lede: Donald Trump has landed in Shenzhen for today's first ever three way meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, though both sides are playing down hopes of big breakthroughs.
Anthropic priced its float at US$83 a share, above its target range, valuing the Claude maker at about US$1.5 trillion before Nasdaq trading starts overnight.
At home, wages grew 1.1% in the September quarter, the fastest pace in nearly three years, but pay is still trailing inflation and the ASX fell again.

stories.h: Trump lands in China for today's meeting with Xi and Putin
stories.b: Trump arrived in Shenzhen on Wednesday morning and was greeted by Xi on the tarmac ahead of APEC. The three way talks with Putin are set for Thursday, alongside a separate Trump and Xi sit down, with nuclear arms limits and Iran expected on the agenda. Both sides hope to extend the US and China trade truce beyond January 2027, but neither has released a formal agenda.
stories.w: Any deal on tariffs or chip curbs between Washington and Beijing flows straight through to demand for Australian iron ore and the wider sharemarket.

stories.h: Expectations stay low for a US and China breakthrough
stories.b: Analysts expect few concrete agreements from the Trump and Xi meeting, and China's own foreign ministry has said hopes for specific outcomes are low. Brookings notes the pair plan to meet again at the G20 in Florida in December, which takes pressure off settling a trade truce extension this week. Progress on military crisis hotlines, including in the nuclear area, is seen as the most likely deliverable.
stories.w: A quiet summit would leave markets guessing on trade into the new year, which is part of why risk appetite has been fragile.

stories.h: Netanyahu's opponents seize control of the Knesset
stories.b: Israel's parliament elected Matan Kahana, from Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party, as speaker by 66 votes to 52, replacing Likud's Amir Ohana. The opposition bloc now controls the chamber's agenda and has named interim chairs for key committees like finance and defence. Likud called it a low point for the Knesset, while Eisenkot still has to build a governing majority.
stories.w: It is the clearest sign yet that Netanyahu's long hold on power is slipping after last month's election, with knock on effects for Gaza and the Iran conflict.

stories.h: COP31 draft deal hits resistance as Friday deadline looms
stories.b: The 18 page draft published by Australia, which is steering talks in Antalya under a shared presidency with Turkey, calls for faster action to move away from coal, oil and gas. The Arab Group and Russia rejected the text outright and the EU's climate envoy said it needed significant changes. A new version is expected before talks are due to close on Friday, and because decisions need consensus, one country can block the lot.
stories.w: Chris Bowen's reputation is tied to the result, and the fossil fuel wording matters for a country that is one of the world's biggest coal and gas exporters.

quick.x: Canada's Mark Carney held a 20 minute meeting with Trump on trade at APEC and agreed further tariff cuts with Xi.
A Russian military transport plane crashed in Siberia, killing 19 people, according to Russia's defence ministry.
The Fed's October minutes leaned hawkish, with a few officials open to a half point hike if inflation data disappoint; markets see a December rise as near certain.

stories.h: Anthropic prices its float above range at US$83 a share
stories.b: Anthropic set its IPO price at US$83, above the US$70 to US$78 range, with the offer reportedly six to seven times oversubscribed. That values the company at about US$1.5 trillion fully diluted, up from US$965 billion in May but short of the US$2 trillion once floated. It sold 825 million shares and trades on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT from Thursday US time.
stories.w: Its debut is a live test of whether investors will still pay up for AI after a bruising few weeks, which matters for super funds heavily exposed to US tech.

stories.h: Nvidia shares slip despite a big beat as the board shuts the door on Huang
stories.b: Nvidia's stock fell 2.9% on Wednesday even after its results and forecast topped estimates, with uncertainty over Jensen Huang's exit weighing. CNBC reported the board is not considering bringing Huang back, despite Trump saying he is open to it and a petition with 180,000 signatures. Interim chief Colette Kress is running the company while law firm Wachtell Lipton investigates Huang's conduct.
stories.w: Nvidia is the bellwether for the whole AI trade, so leadership doubts there ripple into chip, data centre and energy stocks here too.

stories.h: AI is finding security holes faster than companies can fix them
stories.b: Palo Alto Networks boss Nikesh Arora says AI tools now find software flaws faster than firms can patch them, and argues a recent run of outages is no coincidence. He wants a shared clearing house for vulnerabilities and faster rollout of detection rules. In Washington, a bipartisan letter is pushing the White House for a national strategy on AI assisted cyber threats.
stories.w: After last week's Microsoft outage hit the AFP and ASIO, the pressure on Australian agencies and banks to patch at machine speed is only growing.

stories.h: Senate report due on eSafety's online duty of care bill
stories.b: The proposed law would require platforms to find and prevent harm to users before it happens, with fines up to A$109 million for failures. eSafety Commissioner Julie Inman Grant told a Senate inquiry she has seen no sign of platforms over censoring, despite objections from Google, Meta, TikTok and Snap. The committee is due to report on Friday.
stories.w: It would be one of the toughest online safety regimes anywhere, adding to the under 16 social media ban already facing a High Court challenge.

quick.x: US senators have written to the White House urging a national plan against AI assisted cyberattacks amid a string of big outages.

stories.h: Albanese poses alongside Putin and warns Russia ahead of Xi talks
stories.b: The PM landed in China for APEC and appeared in a leaders' photo that included Putin, while restating that the invasion of Ukraine is illegal. He said the Trump, Xi and Putin meeting is not something for Australia to decide. His fifth formal meeting with Xi is on Friday morning, followed by annual talks with Premier Li Qiang in Beijing, with BHP and Rio Tinto among the business delegation.
stories.w: China is Australia's biggest trading partner, and Albanese has said he wants no quotas on Australian goods anywhere.

stories.h: Chalmers lets super funds take bigger bets on housing, energy and startups
stories.b: Under changes to the annual super performance test, funds could put up to 5% of their portfolios into emerging assets benchmarked against inflation instead of market indices. The Treasurer says it could unlock up to $90 billion for things like new housing, energy projects and startups, and insists the test is being strengthened, not watered down. Participation is optional; the industry body ASFA welcomed it, while AustralianSuper said the current test was not holding it back.
stories.w: Your super could end up funding more home building and the energy transition, with a bit more risk but potentially higher long run returns.

stories.h: Gas reservation bill faces its Senate test this week
stories.b: Labor's bill would make the biggest gas exporters set aside up to 20% of output for local users from 2028. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor welcomed the effective carve out for WA, but the Coalition has not committed its votes and the Greens and One Nation are opposed. Labor needs either the Coalition or the Greens to get it through.
stories.w: The scheme is meant to ease east coast gas prices for households and manufacturers, so its fate matters for power bills.

stories.h: Victorian early voting opens with Labor fighting to hang on
stories.b: Early voting began on Wednesday for the 28 November election, with more than 200 centres open for a 10 day window. Polls this year have Labor, the Coalition and One Nation closely bunched on primary votes, and Liberal leader Jess Wilson has led Jacinta Allan as preferred premier. Nearly half of Victorians voted early in 2022.
stories.w: A loss in Victoria, Labor's strongest state, would be a big warning sign for the federal government.

quick.x: Labor lost a Senate floor vote on a bill stopping it reviving its cap on allied health services, sending amendments back to the House.
Chalmers says next month's mid year budget update will include a substantial package of spending cuts.

stories.h: Wages grow at the fastest pace in nearly three years
stories.b: The Wage Price Index rose 1.1% in the September quarter and 3.5% over the year, a touch above forecasts. Private sector pay rose 1.0%, driven by the 4.75% award increase, while public sector pay jumped 1.3% on state deals for nurses, midwives and police. It is the fourth straight quarter of wages lagging inflation, so real pay is still going backwards.
stories.w: Faster wage growth keeps pressure on the RBA, which hiked this month, and makes a rate cut any time soon look less likely.

stories.h: ASX slides again as tech and gold miners drag
stories.b: The ASX 200 fell 61.4 points, or 0.69%, to 8,821.8 on Wednesday, following Wall Street's AI selloff and higher bond yields. Gold miners and tech stocks were hit hardest, while energy and utilities were the only sectors to rise, helped by coal miners. Overnight the Dow fell 1.1% but the Nasdaq edged up 0.4%.
stories.w: That is a second straight weak day after Tuesday's 1.8% drop, and any super fund heavy in Australian shares will feel it.

stories.h: Challenger knocks back a sweetened $12.20 a share bid
stories.b: TAL Daiichi Life, which already owns about a fifth of the annuities provider, raised its offer to $12.20 a share from $11.80 for the rest of the company. Challenger's board says the new price still does not reflect fair value for a full takeover, though talks can continue. The shares last closed at $11.95.
stories.w: Challenger is a major provider of retirement income products, so a Japanese takeover would reshape a key part of the super system.

stories.h: Nuix soars on a US private equity approach
stories.b: US firm Haveli Investments has offered $2.75 a share for the investigative software company, a 73% premium to Tuesday's $1.59 close. The proposal is non binding and subject to due diligence, but the board has granted five weeks of exclusivity and Macquarie, with about 28%, supports the process. The shares jumped about 49%.
stories.w: It is another sign that foreign buyers see beaten down ASX tech stocks as cheap.

quick.x: The Aussie dollar slipped 0.19% to about 67.18 US cents and sits near a 10 month low despite the stronger wages figure.
Brent crude eased to about US$92 a barrel after a 5.28 million barrel build in US stockpiles, with Hormuz risks limiting the fall.
The ABS releases October jobs figures at 11.30am today, after unemployment rose to 4.7% in September.

explainer.body: Before a company lists, its investment banks run a bookbuild, collecting bids from big investors on how many shares they want and at what price. The company first sets an indicative range, like Anthropic's US$70 to US$78. If the book is oversubscribed, meaning bids far exceed the shares on offer, the price can be set above the range, as Anthropic did at US$83. Pricing too high risks a flop on day one, while pricing too low leaves money on the table for the company. That is why a first day jump or slump is watched as a verdict on demand.
